sections.label: Diagnostic characters
sections.text: A small dark brown species. The alate has the head, thorax and abdomen dark brown, the wing veins a lighter brown but darker than the wing membrane, the compound eyes small (0.25×0.29), the antennae 14—16-segmented, and the fore wing scale very large, almost completely covering the hind wing scale. Compared with C. atratus it is larger, with a different pronotum, 1—3 more antennal segments and a wing membrane without spinous microtrichia; compared with C. gearyi (the other dark brown Australian species) it is smaller. The soldier is readily distinguished from all other Australian species by the relatively pale head and the distinctly sloping frons, its head shape resembling that of C. canalensis; in soldiers from New South Wales and Victoria the anterior projections are longer and stouter, and the depression of the frontal projection is especially deep in specimens from Victoria.

sections.label: Alate
sections.text:
A small dark brown species. Head, thorax and abdomen dark brown, the wing veins a lighter brown but darker than the wing membrane. Head small, longer than wide, widest behind the compound eyes, narrowing anteriorly, finely shagreened. Compound eyes small (0.25×0.29) and prominent. Antennae 14—16-segmented. Pronotum large, much wider than the head, distinctly arched, finely shagreened, with depressed margins; the anterior margin broadly concave, the sides, the posterolateral angles and the posterior margin rounded, the middle of the posterior margin slightly concave; the anterior 1/3 bears several deep pits that begin near the midpoint between the mid-line and the lateral margin of the anterior edge and run backwards and obliquely to the mid-line. Fore wing scale very large, almost completely covering the hind wing scale. Wings short; the subcostal vein of the fore wing short, about as long as the width of the wing at the suture; the radial vein more than twice as long as the subcostal.
Measurements: length with wings 8.50 mm; length without wings 5.50 mm; head length (to apex of labrum) 1.25 mm; head length (to clypeofrontal suture) 0.85—0.96 mm; pronotum length 0.63 mm; pronotum width 1.12—1.22 mm; fore wing length 6.00 mm.

sections.label: Soldier
sections.text:
Mandibles, postclypeus and frons black; vertex, palpi and lateral cervical plates dark reddish brown, the occipital region paler. Head short and broad, finely shagreened, the vertex depressed; the frontal projection indistinct except at its two lateral ends, which project and bear a degenerate median cleft; the ventral part of the gena has a short, stout, horn-like prolongation, and there is another slightly larger projection near the lateral margin of the postclypeus. Frons wrinkled and sloping at an angle of 45°. Antennae 13—15-segmented, usually 13, segment 3 short, narrow and dark. Mandibles of medium length, convex externally at the base, with well-developed teeth. Pronotum slightly narrower than the head, the anterior margin broad and deeply concave, slightly serrate.
Measurements: body length (head at right angles to the body) 4.00 mm; head length (to anterior margin of frontal projection) 1.11 mm; head length (to apex of mandibles) 2.03 mm; head width 1.25 mm; pronotum length 0.77 mm; pronotum width 1.22 mm.

note: Rewritten from the English species-level description in Hill (1942); the original gives it as Calotermes (Cryptotermes) queenslandis Hill (the heading line was OCRed as 'Galotermes'), with the synonym line citing 1933 Calotermes (Cryptotermes) queenslandis Hill and the type locality Toowoomba (Qld), also recording Wallaville, Yarraman, Galston (NSW) and Mallacoota (Vic.). The original has only the alate and soldier sections, with no description of the worker. The head length (to anterior margin of frontal projection) was OCRed in the original as 'd.ll' and is read as 1.11 mm, which the lead should verify. OCR misreadings: 'Pigs.'='Figs.', 'Prons'='Frons', 'preminent'='prominent', '13~15'='13-15', 'serra’te'='serrate'; 'obsolescent' and 'shagreened' are terms of the original book.
